title: The Global Sour Barrel
dek: The sour grades WCS competes with, Dubai, Mars, Merey: how they are priced, and what moves the arb.

claims.text: Mars crude, the Louisiana medium sour grade, weakened further against West Texas Intermediate (WTI) as rising shipping costs for US-to-Asia routes narrowed the export arb, per Bloomberg reporting on Sep 24. The move makes freight the deciding variable on whether US Gulf sours clear locally or sail to Asia.

Louisiana-delivered Mars settled at $87.65 per barrel in the March 2026 unwind, down about $20 per barrel from the prior session's Argus outright assessment, after comments from US President Donald Trump that the US-Israel war on Iran could end soon triggered a broad selloff. The volume-weighted average premium over West Texas Intermediate (WTI) fell to $4.20 per barrel, about $8.50 per barrel lower than the prior session, with a high-to-low swing of about $10 per barrel. Mars also narrowed from a roughly $13.80 per barrel premium to June Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) Brent futures to about $2.40 per barrel, and Southern Green Canyon traded as low as parity to Domestic Sweet (DSW) crude at Cushing, down from a $7.07 per barrel premium. The snap-back shows how much of the March premium was war risk rather than physical tightness.

S and P Global Platts data showed the November Brent/Dubai Exchange of Futures for Swaps (EFS) at 4.22 dollars a barrel on Sep 27, up 20 cents from the Sep 24 Asian close and its highest since July 8, when it was pegged at 4.29. Traders linked the climb to surging winter gas prices and expectations of gas-to-oil switching demand, while the October/November Dubai timespread held at a 1.03 dollar a barrel backwardation.

The same reporting noted September spot activity from Japan, India and China was minimal, keeping a lid on cash Dubai premiums despite the EFS strength. An unconfirmed Singapore trader report had October-loading Basrah Heavy sold to private Indian refiners at 50 to 70 cents a barrel below its Official Selling Price (OSP), a sign that physical sour premiums are not following paper.

The Brent-Dubai Exchange of Futures for Swaps (EFS), the spread between Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) Brent futures and Dubai swaps, averaged $1.47 per barrel in the first half of January 2026, surged above $6 per barrel by March 3 as the Hormuz freeze took hold, averaged $9.12 per barrel in March, and oscillated between $3.05 and $16.25 per barrel through June and July. In stable conditions the EFS trades around $1.50 to $2.00 per barrel, and past spikes such as Abqaiq in 2019 and the Russia-Ukraine shock in 2022 barely nudged it above $1.50, making the 2026 move unprecedented in both scale and duration. In 2026 the geographic (routing security) component has overwhelmed the quality component, turning the EFS into a proxy for supply security rather than crude type, and it is the key East-West arb signal for Dubai-basket sour grades.

Reuters reported on Oct 5 that Saudi Aramco set the November Arab Light official selling price (OSP) to Asia at $5.00 per barrel below the Oman/Dubai average, a $3 per barrel cut from October and the widest discount since June 2020, against expectations of a $3 per barrel hike in a Reuters survey. Arab Medium and Arab Heavy were cut by $5 each, while November OSPs for northwest Europe were raised $3 across all grades after exports resumed from the Red Sea port of Yanbu, and US prices were left unchanged. Aramco had looked at offering discounts to compensate buyers for record freight rates and protect market share after the regional conflict hit exports, per people familiar with the matter. This reverses the early-September announcement that had set November Arab Light to Asia at $4.00 per barrel over Oman/Dubai.

Saudi Aramco set its November 2026 official selling prices (OSPs) with Arab Light to East Asia at $4.00 per barrel over the Oman/Dubai average, up from $3.60 for October; to West Europe at $7.20 per barrel over (ICE) Brent, up from $5.70; to the Mediterranean at $6.30 per barrel over (ICE) Brent, up from $4.40; and to North America unchanged at $7.45 per barrel over the Argus Sour Crude Index (ASCI). Arab Medium and Arab Heavy to Asia were held flat at $3.45 and $1.70 over Oman/Dubai. The pattern, much bigger hikes for Europe than for Asia, prices in stronger European competition for sour barrels while testing how much Asian demand can absorb.
claims.vintage: Announced early Sep 2026 for November 2026 loadings; accessed 2026-09-24
claims.source: Argaam (November table; October comparison via Eye of Riyadh)

claims.text: Basra Oil Company chief Bassem Abdul Karim said on Sep 24 that the northern leg now carries about 250,000 barrels per day of Basrah crude to Turkey's Mediterranean port of Ceyhan, while southern terminals handled about 2.6 million barrels per day. The same parliamentary hearing put Iraq's war-related revenue loss near 60 billion dollars and flagged sharply higher shipping costs.

Chatham House analysis published Sep 25 describes a proposed revival of the historic Kirkuk-Baniyas corridor, routed via a new hub at Haditha, that would give Baghdad a 2-million-barrel-per-day Hormuz bypass at an estimated cost near 15 billion dollars and roughly four years of construction, reportedly backed by the Trump administration. The piece cautions it diversifies rather than replaces Hormuz, since most Iraqi barrels are bound for China and India, which sit closer to the Gulf than to the Mediterranean.

The Syrian Petroleum Company's Refining Directorate said the first consignment of about 32,800 metric tons of gasoline arrived by tanker at Baniyas and is moving to the Iraqi border by truck under a transit contract with Qatar's UCC Holding, which supplies the fuel and manages transport. Iraq's Oil Ministry confirmed the arrangement; the deal is gasoline-only for now but the route could later carry crude.
claims.vintage: Week of Sep 21-26, 2026; published Sep 26, 2026; accessed 2026-09-28
claims.source: Freedom Bunker (via The Cradle and Reuters)

claims.text: Iraq's crude exports jumped 73 percent in August 2026 to 73 million barrels for the month (about 2.34 million barrels per day), the highest level since the Iran war began, after the State Organization for Marketing of Oil (SOMO) sold Basrah crude at discounts of $25 to $30 per barrel to offset extreme shipping and insurance costs and a small number of Iraqi tankers received special Iranian permission to transit the Strait of Hormuz. The rebound returned more than $4.5 billion of medium-sour crude to the market in a single month, directly relieving the Dubai-basket sour shortfall that had supported Mars and other Atlantic Basin sours.

Iraq's State Organization for Marketing of Oil (SOMO) offered Basrah Medium and Basrah Heavy for collection by ship-to-ship (STS) transfer near the Omani coast for September delivery via tender, the first time since the Iran war began that buyers could lift Iraqi crude outside the Persian Gulf instead of loading deep inside it. Vitol Group and TotalEnergies were among the largest traders moving Iraqi oil during the war, and SOMO also tendered fuel oil for pickup inside or outside the Gulf. If the outside-Hormuz loading point becomes routine, it structurally lowers the freight risk embedded in Basrah pricing and narrows the crisis premium in Dubai-linked grades.

Sparta Commodities' market outlook dated Sep 30 reported that the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) offered 40 million barrels of sour grades under FY26 RFP #4 for delivery in November and December 2026, split 20 million each from Bryan Mound and Big Hill, with bids due Oct 6. The first replacement window for Bryan Mound is Q2 2027 at a 7.5% volumetric interest rate, and Jun-Sep 2027 at 9.5% for Big Hill, versus a minimum 18% on the earlier FY26 Release #2. Sparta's read is that the release should keep US Gulf Coast medium grades under pressure for the balance of the year, and it looks for Mars December FOB to drop below $1 per barrel, revisiting levels last seen in early August. Treat as a trader outlook, not a newsroom report.

The US government's own sour barrel is shifting grade: DOE's August 20 grade table showed the SPR at 101.8 million barrels sweet and 192.3 million sour, and by September 11 the split was 96.8 million sweet and 188.1 million sour (Reuters), meaning sweet drew about 5.0 million barrels against 4.2 million of sour over roughly three weeks. With the reserve at roughly 34% sweet versus DOE's 40% design target, the government's remaining emergency supply is getting more sour-dominant, which limits how much sweet relief a future release could actually deliver to light-sweet markets.
claims.source: US Department of Energy (SPR Quick Facts); Reuters (via Permian Basin Oil and Gas Magazine)

claims.text: The seven core producers of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC+) and its allies (Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman) met virtually on September 6, 2026 and held October production quotas at September levels, the first month since April without an increase. The decision follows the August 2 approval of a 188,000 barrel per day September increase (Saudi Arabia and Russia 62,000 each, Iraq 26,000, Kuwait 16,000, Kazakhstan 10,000, Algeria 6,000, Oman 5,000), which completed the unwinding of the 2023 voluntary cuts. October required levels: Saudi Arabia 10.478 million barrels per day, Russia 9.949, Iraq 4.431, Kuwait 2.676, Kazakhstan 1.628, Algeria 1.007, Oman 0.841. Delegates expect quotas to hold through year-end while a 2027 baseline review runs; the next review is October 4.
claims.source: NewsGoLive (quoting OPEC statement); September increase detail via World Oil

claims.text: A record 3.5 million barrels per day of US crude was scheduled to arrive in Asia-Pacific for June 2026 delivery, with Japan alone taking more than 530,000 barrels per day versus a prior monthly high of 290,000 in December 2025, as Asian complex refiners substituted Dubai-basket sour grades with Atlantic Basin barrels. India's July arrivals included 2.8 million barrels per day of Russian Urals (over 55 percent of imports), while Reliance's Jamnagar complex took record volumes of Latin American, US and Canadian barrels and blended them to approximate a medium-sour feedstock. The flow shows Asian sour demand leaking out of the Dubai pricing system entirely, which caps how much support the sour complex can draw from Asian buying.
claims.source: Petroleum Economist (citing S&P Global Commodity Insights)

claims.text: US refineries ran at 97 percent utilization in the week ending Sep 11, with no idle capacity left to switch on. US distillate production averaged 5.1 million barrels per day from January through August, the most since 2019, while distillate inventories sat 15.8 million barrels, or 13 percent, below the five-year seasonal average. The read for sour crude: heavy sour barrels with high distillate yields stay bid as long as this lasts.
claims.vintage: Data: week ending Sep 11, 2026; published Sep 21, 2026; accessed 2026-09-28

claims.text: US refinery utilization hit 97.4 percent in late August 2026, the highest since 2018, and shipbroker Gibson reports very little autumn maintenance is confirmed because robust margins keep refiners from taking units offline. The only confirmed turnaround on the Petroleum Administration for Defense District 3 (PADD 3) slate is ExxonMobil's Beaumont fluid catalytic cracking (FCC) unit plus at least two hydrotreaters, running about 45 days from early December to mid-January. PBF pushed Chalmette's crude distillation unit (CDU) and coker into 2027 and CITGO did the same with the Lake Charles coker, while Valero guided third-quarter Gulf Coast throughput at 1.78 to 1.83 million barrels per day. The International Energy Agency (IEA) still expects October North America runs of 18.8 million barrels per day versus 20.5 in August. Sustained near-max runs keep US Gulf Coast (USGC) coker demand for Mars, Western Canadian Select (WCS) and Merey-type barrels elevated, but deferred maintenance raises unplanned-outage risk.

Asian refining margins for 10 parts per million (ppm) sulfur diesel surged to a record just above $87 per barrel in mid-September 2026, versus pre-war levels around $22 per barrel and a prior record of $85.60 set in late March 2026, while the front-month diesel spread stood slightly above $11 per barrel, near a five-month high. Because medium-sour grades carry higher distillate yields than light sweets, record diesel cracks directly support bids for Mars-type barrels and widen the incentive for complex refiners to run heavy sour slates.

Pemex crude exports fell to a 35-year low of about 368,000 barrels per day in December 2025, down 54 percent year over year, as the Olmeca refinery (Dos Bocas) ramped to over 260,000 barrels per day of heavy crude processing and absorbed barrels once destined for export. The export collapse removed roughly 440,000 barrels per day of heavy sour supply year over year, and US imports from Mexico fell to 224,500 barrels per day in December (down 22 percent month over month). With crude production capped at 1.8 million barrels per day under Mexico's Energy Sovereignty 2030 roadmap, the industry may lean more heavily on Western Canadian Select (WCS) or Mars as the Americas heavy benchmark as Maya liquidity dries up.

The Maya export collapse partially reversed as Pemex's refineries stumbled: the Olmeca (Dos Bocas) refinery, with 340,000 barrels per day of nameplate capacity, averaged only 144,000 barrels per day in the second quarter of 2026 (about 42 percent utilization) after a January electrical failure knocked out its coker, catalytic and hydrodesulfurization units, deferring around 150,000 barrels of crude processing. Mexican crude exports averaged about 550,000 barrels per day in March through May 2026, down from roughly 780,000 a year earlier, while fuel imports climbed to 700,000 barrels per day in June. If domestic plants keep underperforming, Maya barrels could swing back onto the US Gulf Coast (USGC) export market, so the heavy-sour shortfall is not one-directional.

OilPrice.com reported on Oct 1 that Venezuela's oil exports fell nearly 9% in September to 1.08 million barrels per day as soaring tanker costs forced Vitol and Trafigura to press PDVSA for steeper discounts and delayed cargoes. US shipments rose to 629,000 barrels per day from 553,000 in August, India fell to 253,000 from 297,000, and European purchases plunged to 86,000 from 260,000. Chevron shipped about 283,000 barrels per day (roughly flat), while trading firms moved 637,000 barrels per day, up from 597,000 in August. Rystad Energy estimates Venezuelan production could reach 1.6 million barrels per day by 2028 and 1.8 million by 2030, but notes the country had only two active drilling rigs in August versus an estimated 50 needed by 2028.

The Western Canadian Select (WCS) discount to West Texas Intermediate (WTI) stood at 21 dollars a barrel on Sep 21, per Argus market reporting, an unusually wide differential for 2026. With Friday's WTI settlement at 92.44 dollars, implied WCS was 71.44 dollars a barrel, down about 7.09 dollars on the week as the Brent-WTI spread hit 11.93 dollars, its widest of 2026. Goldman Sachs' fourth-quarter 2026 Brent target of 85 dollars a barrel translates to WCS near 59 dollars, roughly 12.44 dollars below the current implied level.
claims.source: Oil Authority (citing Argus and Goldman Sachs)

claims.text: An infographic from Modern Miracle Network, citing Bloomberg and Argus data, says zero percent of Vancouver-to-Asia crude used the Southern California ship-to-ship transfer to very large crude carriers in August 2026, versus 78 percent in June 2024, with direct Aframax shipments across the Pacific costing about 54 percent of the California-transfer route. Treat as an unconfirmed lead: the economics are plausible given elevated very large crude carrier rates, but it comes from an advocacy account, not a newsroom.

Western Canadian Select (WCS) at Hardisty, Alberta traded at an $8.50 per barrel discount to West Texas Intermediate (WTI) on June 2, 2026, tightening from $9.75 on May 26, as wildfires shut in nearly 350,000 barrels per day of Canadian output (Cenovus's Christina Lake alone lost about 238,000 barrels per day). S&P Global Commodity Insights analysts noted that lower volumes from Mexico and Venezuela to the US Gulf Coast (USGC) have also limited heavy sour supply, and that Chevron's exit from Venezuela was expected to pull up to 200,000 barrels per day of heavy crude from the USGC. The episode shows WCS pricing off the same shrinking USGC heavy-sour pool that Mars and Merey serve.
